title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others

Whether the driver of the offending vehicle holding a valid driving license for HGV/HTV required a special endorsement to drive a goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods (Tanker) under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, and whether its absence constitutes a breach entitling the insurance company to recovery rights

ratio: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license as prescribed under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach of insurance policy terms entitling the insurer to pay and recover.

A vehicle designed as a tanker carrying hazardous/dangerous goods requires a special endorsement on the driver's license under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989.

court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao
bench: Devi Prasad Singh, Dr. Satish Chandra
legal_issues: Whether the insurance company is liable to pay compensation when the tractor is insured but the attached trolley/trailer is not separately insured
Whether transporting bricks and iron rods in a tractor trolley constitutes a violation of the terms and conditions of an insurance policy restricted to agricultural purposes

holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

key_principles: A trailer is an attachment with no independent propulsion and its insurance is not a mandatory separate requirement if the prime mover tractor is insured.

legal_issues: Whether the insurer is liable to pay compensation when the driver's driving license had expired prior to the accident and was renewed subsequently after more than 30 days?
Whether the principle of 'pay and recover' applies in cases where the driver did not hold a valid and effective driving license on the date of the accident?

ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.
disposition: Appeal allowed. The judgment and award of the Tribunal are modified; liability is fastened on the owner of the offending vehicle, but the Insurance Company is directed to pay the compensation to the claimants and recover the same from the insured in the same proceedings.
key_principles: Under Section 15 of the Motor Vehicles Act, if an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed with effect from the date of its renewal and is not retrospective.

Driving a vehicle with an expired license where renewal is sought beyond 30 days means the driver did not possess a valid and effective driving license on the date of an accident occurring during the interim period.

court: Supreme Court of India
legal_issues: Whether the appellant's conviction under Section 304A IPC is sustainable when a passenger falls from a moving bus while boarding and there is no evidence of negligent driving.
holding: The conviction of the appellant under Section 304A IPC is unsustainable due to scanty evidence regarding negligent driving, and the appeal is allowed by setting aside the conviction and sentence.
ratio: Negligence of a driver cannot be presumed merely because a passenger fell down from a bus while boarding; there must be direct evidence establishing that the driver moved the vehicle suddenly or without proper signals before criminal negligence can be fastened.
disposition: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, and the appellant acquitted.
key_principles: Negligence of a driver cannot be presumed for any motor accident without evidence.

The principle of res ipsa loquitur applies only when the nature of the accident and circumstances reasonably lead to the belief that it would not have occurred without negligence and the instrumentality was under the management of the wrongdoer.

Mrs Sudha Rasheed v. Union of India
holding: The State is liable under public law jurisdiction for breach of Article 21 when it fails to protect a citizen from a terrorist attack, and must pay monetary compensation to the victim's dependents.
ratio: When an innocent citizen's fundamental right to life under Article 21 is violated due to the State's failure to prevent a crime or terrorist act, the High Court under Article 226 can award public law compensation based on strict liability, comprising standard non-pecuniary compensation and pecuniary dependency loss calculated via the multiplier method.
disposition: Writ petition disposed of with a direction to the respondents to pay Rs 4,36,500/- along with simple interest at 7% per annum from 20.4.1996 to the petitioner within four weeks.
key_principles: State is liable under strict liability in public law for breach of Article 21 when it fails to protect citizens from terrorist acts.
Relegating crime victims to ordinary civil courts for tort remedies is inadequate; High Courts under Article 226 have plenary power to grant compensation.
Compensation consists of a standard/conventional amount for non-pecuniary losses (adjusted for inflation) and pecuniary dependency loss using the multiplier method.

ratio: Public law remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is available to award monetary compensation for the violation of the fundamental right to life under Article 21 resulting from gross medical negligence by state-employed medical professionals, and the defense of sovereign immunity is inapplicable to such strict liability claims.
disposition: Writ petition allowed
key_principles: Principle of res ipsa loquitur applies to medical negligence cases where surgical mops are left inside a patient's abdomen.
Violation of fundamental rights through gross negligence by public officials gives rise to a constitutional tort.
The defense of sovereign immunity is alien to constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226 for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
Monetary compensation in public law acts as a palliative and is distinct from, and in addition to, private law remedies in tort.

court: In The Court Of The Ix Addl. Small Causes And Addl. Mact., Bangalore, (Scch-7)
legal_issues: Whether the petitioners prove they are the dependents and legal representatives of the deceased Sri. M. Eshwarappa?
Whether the petitioners prove the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the bus bearing registration no. KA-51-C-114 by its driver, resulting in the death of Sri. M. Eshwarappa?
Whether the petitioners are entitled to compensation, and if so, how much and from whom?
precedents_cited: Rajesh and Others V/s. Rajbir Singh and Others

Smt. Sarla Verma and Others V/s. Delhi Transport Corporation and Another

holding: The tribunal held that the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the offending bus, and awarded compensation of Rs. 25,95,346/- with interest at 9% p.a. to be paid by the insurer.
ratio: In fatal accident compensation claims under the Motor Vehicles Act, when the deceased is below 40 years of age and in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects.
disposition: Petition allowed in part with costs; respondents No. 1 and 2 are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation, with respondent No. 1 directed to deposit the amount.
key_principles: Just compensation must be awarded irrespective of the amount claimed.
Fathers cannot generally be considered dependent on their adult sons in motor accident claims.
Addition towards future prospects applies to persons below 40 years with regular employment.

title: Nazar Singh vs State Of Punjab And Others
court: In The High Court For The States Of Punjab And Haryana At Chandigarh
legal_issues: Whether an employer can recover compensation paid to third-party motor accident victims from its employee-driver without holding a proper departmental inquiry and affording an effective opportunity of hearing.
Whether the State as owner of an un-insured vehicle can recover compensation amounts from the driver when it failed to establish a statutory fund under Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
precedents_cited: State of Maharashtra and others v. Kanchanmala Vijaysing Shirke and others
HC Dilbagh Singh v. State of Punjab
holding: The court held that an employer cannot recover compensation paid to accident victims from its employee-driver based solely on a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal award without conducting a departmental inquiry, establishing fault through due process, and providing an effective opportunity of hearing.
ratio: An employer cannot effect recovery of compensation paid to third-party victims from an employee-driver without conducting a departmental inquiry adhering to principles of natural justice and without establishing the employee's liability through proper procedure.
disposition: Petition allowed and the recovery order dated 24.2.1994 is quashed.
key_principles: Vicarious liability of the State to pay compensation awarded is qua the claimants and not qua the employee-driver.

Recovery of loss from an employee-driver requires a prior departmental inquiry and compliance with the principles of natural justice, and a Tribunal award alone cannot form the sole basis for recovery without independent inquiry.
State transport undertakings must either insure their vehicles or maintain a statutory fund under Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to meet third-party liabilities.

title: Jagdish Rai vs State Of Punjab And Others
court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh
legal_issues: Whether the recovery of a motor accident compensation amount from a government driver's salary without holding a disciplinary inquiry as required under the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970 is legally sustainable.
statutes_cited: Rule 5, Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules 1970
Rule 10, Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules 1970
precedents_cited: Sahi Ram and another Vs. State of Haryana through Collector, District Mohindergarh and others
The General Manager, Kerala State Road Transport Corporation, Trivandrum Vs. Mrs. Susamma Thomas and others
Ajaib Singh v. State of Punjab
State of Maharashtra v. Kanchanmala Vijaysing Shirke
holding: The court held that the order directing recovery from the petitioner's salary without following the procedure for imposing minor penalties under Rule 10 of the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970 is illegal and must be set aside, while granting liberty to the respondents to proceed in accordance with law.
ratio: Recovery from the pay of a government employee for pecuniary loss caused by negligence is a minor penalty under service rules and cannot be imposed without complying with the mandatory procedural requirements of issuing a notice and providing an opportunity of hearing and inquiry under Rule 10.
disposition: Petition allowed; impugned recovery order quashed with liberty to respondents to proceed in accordance with law.
key_principles: Vicarious liability of the employer for acts of the servant in course of employment
Mandatory nature of disciplinary procedure and rules of natural justice before imposing minor penalties involving pecuniary recovery from government employees

title: Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd vs C.C.E., Raipur
court: Customs Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
legal_issues: Whether Cenvat credit of service tax is admissible on marine inland transit insurance for capital goods of a captive power plant
Whether Cenvat credit is admissible on insurance for money in transit from factory to bank
Whether Cenvat credit is admissible on follow-up services for installation of a captive power plant
Whether Cenvat credit is admissible on telephone services installed at the residence of the General Manager and the company's guest house
Whether Cenvat credit is admissible on insurance premiums for personnel working in the factory (including contract workers)
precedents_cited: C.C.E., Mumbai V vs. GTC Industries Ltd.
Finolex Cables Ltd. vs. C.C.E., Pune I
Millipore India Ltd. vs. C.C.E., Bangalore II
holding: The Tribunal held that Cenvat credit is admissible on transit insurance of plant and machinery, money in transit insurance, follow-up services for installation, and personnel accident insurance, but is rightly denied in respect of telephone services installed at the General Manager's residence and the company's guest house.
ratio: Since inward transportation of inputs or capital goods is covered under the definition of 'input service', transit insurance of capital goods during transportation, insurance of money in transit for business operations, installation-related services, and personnel accident insurance for workers in the factory form part of business activities and qualify as input services under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.
disposition: Appeal allowed in part, setting aside the denial of cenvat credit and penalty except with respect to the telephone services at the General Manager's residence and guest house.
key_principles: Inward transportation and associated transit insurance of capital goods are covered within the definition of input services.
Insurance of money in transit for day-to-day business operations qualifies as an input service.
Services relating to setting up or modernization, such as follow-up services for installation of a captive power plant, are eligible for Cenvat credit.
Medical, personal accident, and group personal accident policies for personnel working in the factory (including contract workers) are covered under input services.
Telephone services at a residence or guest house not shown to be used in manufacturing business are ineligible for Cenvat credit.

title: K. Surappa vs V. Venkatesha Reddy And Others
court: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal
legal_issues: Whether the relationship of master and servant between the vehicle owner and driver ceases or is suspended when the vehicle is requisitioned for election purposes under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act.
Whether the State is liable or entitled to sovereign immunity for the tortious act of the driver when the vehicle is requisitioned for election purposes.
Whether the insurer can avoid liability to pay compensation on the ground that the vehicle was commandeered for election purposes.
statutes_cited: Section 160, Representation of the People Act
Section 161, Representation of the People Act
precedents_cited: Mersey Docks and Harbour Board v. Coggins & Griffith (Liverpool) Ltd.
Bhoomidas v Port of Singapore Authority
holding: The court held that requisitioning a vehicle along with its driver under the Representation of the People Act does not terminate or suspend the master-servant relationship between the owner and the driver, and the owner remains vicariously liable for the driver's negligence.
ratio: The requisitioning of a vehicle under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act, where hire charges are paid but the services of the driver are not separately requisitioned or paid for, does not suspend the relationship of master and servant between the vehicle owner and the driver; hence, the owner remains vicariously liable for the tortious acts of the driver.
disposition: Appeal allowed with costs. The judgment and award of the Tribunal rejecting the appellant's claim are set aside. The petition is allowed in part, awarding Rs. 20,000/- with interest at 12% per annum, with the insurer liable for Rs. 5,000/- and the first respondent-owner liable for the balance.
key_principles: Requisitioning a vehicle under the Representation of the People Act is akin to taking a vehicle on hire, which does not terminate the employment relationship between the owner and the driver unless the hirer assumes the payment of wages.

The general employer bears a heavy burden to prove a transfer of service of an employee, which is not established merely because the hirer or requisitioning authority gives directions as to when and where the vehicle is to be taken.

title: Ajay Alias Vishal Veeru Devgan vs The Artists Planet & Ors
court: In The High Court Of Delhi At New Delhi
case_type: civil - personality and publicity rights infringement
legal_issues: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to an ex-parte ad-interim injunction protecting his personality, publicity, and moral rights against unauthorized commercial exploitation and AI-generated deepfakes.
Whether social media intermediaries and domain registrars are liable to take down infringing content and disclose basic subscriber information.

ratio: A well-known celebrity or public figure inherently possesses proprietary personality and publicity rights over their name, image, voice, and likeness, entitling them to seek an interim injunction against unauthorized commercial exploitation, merchandising, and the generation of deceptive or obscene deepfake content using artificial intelligence.
disposition: Allowed in part (ex-parte ad-interim injunction granted with specific directions for takedown, compliance affidavits, and further proceedings).
key_principles: Protection of celebrity personality and publicity rights under common law and Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution.
Restraint against unauthorized commercial exploitation, merchandising, and AI-generated deepfakes or face-morphing.
Obligation of litigants to utilize statutory grievance redressal mechanisms under the IT Intermediary Rules before seeking ex-parte injunctions in certain contexts.

title: New Balance Athletics Inc. vs Ashok Kumar & Ors.
court: In The High Court Of Delhi At New Delhi
legal_issues: Whether the defendants' sale of counterfeit products bearing the plaintiff's registered trademarks amounts to trademark infringement and passing off.
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to a decree of permanent injunction and actual costs for trademark infringement.
statutes_cited: Order I Rule 10 (2), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Order VIII Rule 10, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
precedents_cited: Puma SE Versus Brijendra Singh trading AS Sastajoota
Jawed Ansari v. Louis Vuitton Malletier
holding: The court decreed the suit in favor of the plaintiff and against defendant nos. 1 and 11 for trademark infringement and passing off, awarding actual litigation costs.
ratio: Where defendants use identical marks on identical goods and target the same consumer base, satisfying the triple identity test and admitting to selling counterfeit products, a case of trademark infringement and passing off is established, warranting a decree under Order VIII Rule 10 CPC.
disposition: Suit decreed in favour of the plaintiff and against defendant nos. 1 and 11.
key_principles: Counterfeiting is a serious economic offence that erodes brand value and misleads consumers, and must be dealt with strictly.
Where the contesting defendants fail to file a written statement, the assertions in the plaint stand admitted, empowering the court to proceed under Order VIII Rule 10 CPC.

title: Azuga Inc & Anr vs Azuga Telematics Llc & Ors
court: In The High Court Of Delhi At New Delhi
legal_issues: Whether the defendants' use of the trademark 'AZUGA' and trade name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' constitutes trademark infringement and passing off.
Whether copying the UI assets and product photographs from the plaintiffs' website constitutes copyright infringement.
statutes_cited: Order XI Rule 1(4), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Order XI Rule 1, 3 and 5, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
holding: The court granted an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining the defendants from using the plaintiffs' registered trademark 'AZUGA' or trade name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS', infringing their copyright in website images, and directing the domain registrar to suspend the infringing domain name.
ratio: Where a plaintiff establishes a prima facie case of unauthorized adoption of a registered trademark and copyright-protected website assets for identical services by former employees and related entities, an ad-interim injunction is warranted to prevent consumer confusion and reputational dilution.
disposition: Application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC allowed; ad-interim injunction granted.
key_principles: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable harm govern the grant of ad-interim injunctions in intellectual property matters.
Adoption of an identical or deceptively similar trademark for identical services by former employees gives rise to a presumption of mala fide intent.

Passing off

title: M/S. Mandvi Co-Op Bank Ltd vs Nimesh B.Thakore
court: Supreme Court Of India
legal_issues: Whether sub-section (2) of section 145 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, confers an unfettered right on the accused to insist that the complainant or his witness must first give deposition in examination-in-chief before being cross-examined.
Whether the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 145 of the Act apply to proceedings pending on the date they came into force.
Whether the right to give evidence on affidavit provided to the complainant under section 145(1) is also available to the accused.
precedents_cited: Dental Council of India vs. Hari Prakash and Ors.
Nathi Devi vs. Radha Devi
Raghunath Rai Bareja vs. Punjab National Bank

holding: The Supreme Court held that under Section 145(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, an accused can only subject the deponent of an affidavit to cross-examination and cannot insist on a fresh examination-in-chief, that the provisions of Section 143 to 147 are procedural and apply retrospectively to pending cases, and that the accused does not have the right under the Act to give evidence on affidavit.
ratio: Under Section 145(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, when a complainant or witness gives evidence on affidavit, an accused who summons them has the right to cross-examine them on the facts stated therein without requiring a fresh examination-in-chief, and the statute does not permit the accused to tender their own defense evidence on affidavit.

title: Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State (Govt. Of Nct Delhi) & Anr.
court: In The High Court Of Delhi At New Delhi
legal_issues: Whether criminal proceedings relating to non-compoundable, heinous, serious, or economic offences can be quashed under Section 482 Cr.P.C. on the basis of a settlement or mediation agreement.
Whether courts and mediation centres should refer criminal cases involving serious or economic offences to mediation without preliminary scrutiny.

K Srinivas Rao vs. D.A. Deepa

Accused persons cannot be permitted to abuse the judicial process to cause protracted delays and then use such delay as a ground to seek settlements and quashing.

title: Company Of Management For Baranagar ... vs Atis Dipankar Chowdhuri
court: High Court of Calcutta
legal_issues: Whether Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act prohibits presenting a dishonoured cheque to the bank for payment more than once.
Whether a Committee of Management appointed by the High Court under a scheme can be prosecuted without the prior leave of the Court.
Whether a Committee of Management constituted under a court-approved scheme falls within the definition of a 'company' under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
precedents_cited: Kumaresan v. Ameerappa
Prithviraj v. Mathew Kashy
Paramjit Singh v. Job
Sarbnarayan Jha v. M/s. Khan Palchowdhury & Co. Pvt. Ltd.
Sekhar Gupta v. Subhas Chandra Mandal

holding: The Court held that while Section 138 does not prohibit presenting a cheque more than once, the criminal proceeding must be quashed because the Committee of Management is a representative of the Court requiring prior leave to prosecute, and it does not constitute a 'company' or 'association of individuals' attracting vicarious liability under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
ratio: A Committee of Management appointed by the High Court functions as an officer or representative of the Court and cannot be prosecuted without prior leave of the appointing Court, nor does it qualify as a company or corporate body subject to criminal prosecution under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

A committee of management created by court order for administering an institution functions as an officer of the court and cannot be criminally prosecuted without the leave of the appointing court.

Whether an appellate court can interfere with a discretionary interlocutory order passed by the trial court under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Order 43 Rule 1(r) of the CPC.

key_principles: Interference with a discretionary interlocutory injunction under Order 43 Rule 1(r) is warranted only in cases of perversity or arbitrariness.
Unless and until a case of irreparable loss or damage is made out, the court should not permit the alienation or transfer of property that may lead to multiplicity of proceedings.
A purchaser pendente lite with notice of a prior agreement to sell cannot be considered a bona fide purchaser under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act.

title: Chinnasamy vs K.Viswanathan(Died)
court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Madras
legal_issues: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to specific performance of the sale agreement when the plaintiff failed to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.
statutes_cited: Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act
Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act
precedents_cited: R.K.Mohammed Ubaidullah & Ors Vs. Hajee C.Abdul Wahab(D) & Ors
Padmakumari & Ors Vs. Dasayyan & Others
holding: The High Court dismissed the second appeal and upheld the lower appellate court's judgment dismissing the plaintiff's suit for specific performance due to lack of proof of readiness and willingness.
ratio: A plaintiff seeking the equitable relief of specific performance must independently plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract in terms of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act.
disposition: dismissed
key_principles: Specific performance is a discretionary equitable relief requiring the plaintiff to satisfy the conscience of the court.
The statutory burden under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act mandates that the plaintiff plead and prove readiness and willingness.

title: Smt Iravva K Purantar vs S Venkatesh
court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
legal_issues: Whether the appellant, who claims through a registered lease-cum-sale agreement executed prior to the institution of the suit and was not originally impleaded, is a proper and necessary party to a suit for specific performance.
Whether the trial court's judgment and decree ought to be set aside and the matter remanded for fresh consideration after permitting impleadment and additional evidence.
holding: The appellate court set aside the trial court's judgment and decree, allowed the appellant to be impleaded as an additional defendant, received additional documents on record, and remanded the matter back to the trial court for a fresh trial and disposal in accordance with law.
ratio: When a third party claims a preexisting right, title, or interest in the suit schedule property through a registered instrument executed by the defendant prior to the institution of the suit, and the defendant fails to contest the suit or cross-examine witnesses, such third party is a proper and necessary party who must be permitted to implead and contest the matter on merits, warranting a remand of the case.
disposition: Appeal allowed. Judgment and decree set aside. Matter remanded to the trial court for fresh consideration after impleadment of the appellant as additional defendant No. 2.
key_principles: A third party holding a prior registered agreement or title from a defendant in a specific performance suit is a proper and necessary party if their rights would be prejudicially affected.

Appellate courts may permit additional documents under Order 41 Rule 27 and remand matters under Order 41 Rule 28 when a party was improperly shut out or unrepresented due to lack of due diligence by a defendant.

title: Kum.H.Supriya vs S Krishnappa
court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
legal_issues: Whether the trial court erred in rejecting the application for amendment of the written statement seeking to incorporate subsequent events.
statutes_cited: Order 6 Rule 17, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
precedents_cited: LIC v. Sanjeev Builders (P) Ltd.
Dinesh Goyal @ pappu v. Suman Agarwal (bindal) & ors.
Shri Mohammadrafi and Anr., Vs. Bandenawaz and Ors
holding: The trial court's order rejecting the application to amend the written statement to include subsequent events is set aside, and the application is allowed.
ratio: Subsequent events occurring after the institution of a suit that could not have been pleaded at the time of filing the written statement should generally be permitted by way of amendment, and the refusal to do so based strictly on lack of due diligence regarding such subsequent events causes a failure of justice.
disposition: Petition allowed; impugned order set aside; I.A.No.VIII allowed.
key_principles: Amendments incorporating subsequent events should be allowed where no prejudice is caused to the opposing party.
